claim: The destabilizing domain (DD) derived from E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (ecDHFR) can control protein stability in a ligand-inducible manner in Drosophila.
source: We adopted the destabilizing domain (DD) derived from dihydrofolate reductase (ecDHFR) of E. coli to control protein stability in a ligand-inducible manner (Cho et al., 2013; Iwamoto et al., 2010), a strategy that has been used to control gene expression in mice and worms (Cho et al., 2013; Iwamoto et al., 2010; Sando et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cho et al., 2013; Iwamoto et al., 2010; Sando et al., 2013) that demonstrated this technology in other organisms.

claim: When DD is fused to a protein of interest, the chimeric protein is degraded by the proteasome.
source: On fusing the destabilizing domain to a protein of interest, the chimeric protein is degraded by the proteasome, but its degradation is blocked by trimethoprim (TMP), a cell-permeable ligand for DD (Figure 1A) (Iwamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iwamoto et al., 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the mechanism.

claim: Trimethoprim (TMP) blocks the degradation of DD-fusion proteins.
source: On fusing the destabilizing domain to a protein of interest, the chimeric protein is degraded by the proteasome, but its degradation is blocked by trimethoprim (TMP), a cell-permeable ligand for DD (Figure 1A) (Iwamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iwamoto et al., 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: TMP is a cell-permeable ligand for the destabilizing domain.
source: On fusing the destabilizing domain to a protein of interest, the chimeric protein is degraded by the proteasome, but its degradation is blocked by trimethoprim (TMP), a cell-permeable ligand for DD (Figure 1A) (Iwamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iwamoto et al., 2010.

claim: Flies fed with TMP show robust GFP-DD expression throughout the brain when using pan-neuronal nsyb-GAL4 driver.
source: Using the pan-neuronal nsyb-GAL4 to drive GFP-DD expression, we observed robust GFP expression throughout the brain of adult flies fed with TMP (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the absence of TMP, GFP-DD expression is low throughout the brain.
source: In the absence of TMP, GFP expression was low throughout the brain; this is consistent with the previous studies in mice and nematodes showing that unbound DD is an effective tag to mark the fusion protein for degradation (Cho et al., 2013; Sando et al., 2013) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and citations to previous studies in other organisms (Cho et al., 2013; Sando et al., 2013).

claim: Unbound DD is an effective tag to mark fusion proteins for degradation in mice and nematodes.
source: In the absence of TMP, GFP expression was low throughout the brain; this is consistent with the previous studies in mice and nematodes showing that unbound DD is an effective tag to mark the fusion protein for degradation (Cho et al., 2013; Sando et al., 2013) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cho et al., 2013; Sando et al., 2013).

claim: TMP-dependent GFP-DD stabilization shows substantial differences between solvent and TMP feeding during larval stage (44-fold difference).
source: We found substantial differences in GFP-DD expression between flies fed with solvent versus TMP during the larval (44 fold), 48 hr APF (19 fold) and three day old adult (27 fold) stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data comparing solvent and TMP feeding conditions.

claim: TMP-dependent GFP-DD stabilization shows a 19-fold difference between solvent and TMP feeding at 48 hr APF.
source: We found substantial differences in GFP-DD expression between flies fed with solvent versus TMP during the larval (44 fold), 48 hr APF (19 fold) and three day old adult (27 fold) stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: TMP-dependent GFP-DD stabilization shows a 27-fold difference between solvent and TMP feeding in three day old adults.
source: We found substantial differences in GFP-DD expression between flies fed with solvent versus TMP during the larval (44 fold), 48 hr APF (19 fold) and three day old adult (27 fold) stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: During late pupal stage (96 hr APF) and eclosion (<12 hr adult), there is a five-fold difference in GFP-DD expression between flies raised on solvent versus TMP.
source: Notably, even though flies do not feed for several days leading up to the late pupal stage (96 hr APF) and eclosion (<12 hr adult), we observed a five-fold difference in GFP-DD expression between flies raised on solvent versus TMP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Flies do not feed for several days leading up to the late pupal stage (96 hr APF) and eclosion.
source: Notably, even though flies do not feed for several days leading up to the late pupal stage (96 hr APF) and eclosion (<12 hr adult), we observed a five-fold difference in GFP-DD expression between flies raised on solvent versus TMP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: The TMP-inducible DD system is maximally effective during the larval, early pupal and adult stages.
source: In summary, the TMP-inducible DD system is maximally effective during the larval, early pupal and adult stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing fold-differences in GFP-DD expression across developmental stages.

claim: During the late pupal stage, the utility of the DD system may be limited by unavailability of TMP.
source: During the late pupal stage, however, the utility of the system may be limited by unavailability of TMP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that flies do not feed during this stage and the reduced fold-difference in expression.

claim: TMP-dependent protein stabilization is compatible with any GAL4, LexA, QF or split-GAL4 line because it acts through post-translational modification.
source: Because TMP-dependent protein stabilization acts through post-translational modification of protein levels, it should be compatible with any GAL4, LexA, QF or split-GAL4 line.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the mechanism of action (post-translational control).

claim: Significant differences in GFP-DD expression (ranging from 4 to 64 fold) were observed between solvent and TMP feeding for every cell type tested.
source: We observed a significant difference in GFP-DD expression (ranging from 4 to 64 fold) between solvent and TMP feeding for every cell type that we tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple cell types.

claim: Maximum differences in GFP-DD expression were observed in the axon terminals of sensory neurons (at least 45 fold).
source: Maximum differences were observed in the axon terminals of sensory neurons (at least 45 fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons showed a much larger difference between TMP and solvent feeding (45 fold) compared to olfactory projection neurons (6 fold), even though both cell types innervate the antennal lobe.
source: For example, olfactory sensory neurons showed a much larger difference between TMP and solvent feeding (45 fold) compared to olfactory projection neurons (6 fold), even though both cell types innervate the antennal lobe.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing two cell types.

claim: PAM dopamine neurons showed a larger difference in GFP-DD expression (12 fold) compared to Kenyon cells (4 fold), even though both cell types innervate the mushroom body.
source: Similarly, PAM dopamine neurons showed a larger difference in GFP-DD expression (12 fold) compared to Kenyon cells (4 fold), even though both cell types innervate the mushroom body.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing two cell types.

claim: At least some of the differences between cell types in DD system effectiveness arise from variability in their proteasome activity levels.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that at least some of the differences between cell types arise from the variability in their proteasome activity levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different cell types show different fold-changes in expression.

claim: The DD system is effective in non-neuronal tissues such as ovaries.
source: We also observed that the DD system was effective in non-neuronal tissues, such as ovaries (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The DD system can be used in combination with the LexA/LexAop binary system.
source: Finally, to demonstrate that the DD system can be used in combination with other binary systems apart from GAL4/UAS, we generated a 13XLexAop-GFP-DD transgenic fly line and observed similar TMP-dependent GFP expression in olfactory sensory neurons using the Orco-LexA driver line (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Feeding adult flies with food containing varying concentrations (0–5 mM) of TMP for 48 hr results in a dose-dependent change in GFP expression in the antennal lobe.
source: Feeding adult flies with food containing varying concentrations (0–5 mM) of TMP for 48 hr resulted in a dose-dependent change in GFP expression in the antennal lobe (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The maximum GFP expression induced by 1 mM TMP was between 34 and 45 times higher than that of control flies fed with solvent-containing food.
source: The maximum GFP expression, induced by 1 mM TMP, was between 34 and 45 times higher than that of control flies fed with the solvent-containing food (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: GFP levels increase initially but plateau within 36 hr when flies are fed with food containing 1 mM TMP for varying durations (0–60 hr).
source: Results from an experiment in which flies were fed for varying durations (0–60 hr) with food containing 1 mM TMP show that GFP levels increase initially but plateau within 36 hr (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: GFP intensity is reduced by 73% within 24 hr after switching flies from TMP-containing food to regular food.
source: To test if TMP-dependent GFP expression is reversible, we fed flies with food containing 1 mM TMP for 48 hr and then switched them to regular food (Figure 1G). We found that the GFP intensity was reduced by 73% within 24 hr (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Genetic fusion of the ecDHFR-derived destabilizing domain confers instability to a protein of interest in Drosophila.
source: In sum, using GFP as a test molecule, we show that genetic fusion of the ecDHFR-derived destabilizing domain confers instability to a protein of interest in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing low GFP expression without TMP and high expression with TMP.

claim: Feeding flies with TMP can control protein levels in a reversible and dose-dependent manner with a large dynamic range.
source: Feeding flies with TMP can control protein levels in a reversible and dose-dependent manner with a large dynamic range.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependency (Figure 1C,D) and reversibility (Figure 1G,H).

claim: Feeding adult flies with TMP ranging from 0 to 10 mM does not have any detectable effect on their survival.
source: Feeding adult flies with a defined medium containing TMP ranging from 0 to 10 mM did not have any detectable effect on their survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Feeding adult flies with 1 mM TMP for 48 hr does not alter their locomotion speed.
source: Moreover, feeding adult flies with 1 mM TMP for 48 hr did not alter their locomotion speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) or their ability to locate an odor source (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) during foraging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Feeding adult flies with 1 mM TMP for 48 hr does not alter their ability to locate an odor source during foraging.
source: Moreover, feeding adult flies with 1 mM TMP for 48 hr did not alter their locomotion speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) or their ability to locate an odor source (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D) during foraging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Flies raised on TMP ranging from 0 to 10 mM throughout development are equally likely to survive to adulthood.
source: Flies raised on TMP ranging from 0 to 10 mM throughout development were equally likely to survive to adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Flies raised on 1 mM TMP show a delay in developmental time (11.2 ± 0.1 days to eclosion) compared to solvent (10.2 ± 0.1 days).
source: However, we observed a delay in the developmental time for flies raised on 1 mM TMP (11.2 ± 0.1 days to eclosion) and 10 mM TMP (15.3 ± 0.3 days) as compared to solvent (10.2 ± 0.1 days) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Flies raised on 10 mM TMP show a delay in developmental time (15.3 ± 0.3 days to eclosion) compared to solvent (10.2 ± 0.1 days).
source: However, we observed a delay in the developmental time for flies raised on 1 mM TMP (11.2 ± 0.1 days to eclosion) and 10 mM TMP (15.3 ± 0.3 days) as compared to solvent (10.2 ± 0.1 days) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Feeding adult flies TMP at 1 mM can induce GFP-DD expression at saturation level without any observable side effects on their survival or behavior.
source: In summary, feeding adult flies TMP at 1 mM can induce GFP-DD expression at saturation level (Figure 1D) without any observable side effects on their survival or behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing saturation at 1 mM (Figure 1D) and no effects on survival or behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: 1 mM TMP delays development by about one day.
source: Notably, however, the same dosage of TMP delays development by about one day.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing developmental delay.

claim: Binding of GAL80 to GAL4 prevents GAL4-mediated transcriptional activation in the GAL4/UAS expression system.
source: Binding of GAL80 to GAL4 prevents GAL4-mediated transcriptional activation in the GAL4/UAS expression system (Lee and Luo, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee and Luo, 1999.

claim: nsyb-GAL80-DD is able to suppress GAL4-dependent GFP expression in olfactory sensory neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that nsyb-GAL80-DD was able to suppress GAL4-dependent GFP expression in olfactory sensory neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The suppression of GFP expression by nsyb-GAL80-DD in flies carrying Orco-GAL4, UAS-GFP and nsyb-GAL80-DD transgenes is TMP-dependent.
source: This suppression of GFP expression in flies carrying the Orco-GAL4, UAS-GFP and nsyb-GAL80-DD transgenes was TMP-dependent (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When flies are moved from TMP-containing food to regular food, GFP expression starts to increase after 24 hr and peaks at 72 hr post-TMP removal.
source: When flies were moved from TMP-containing food to regular food, GFP expression started to increase after 24 hr, and peaked at 72 hr post-TMP removal (Figure 2B1, C1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B1, C1.

claim: Flies fed with TMP continuously from embryo to adult show low GFP expression throughout the experiment.
source: In contrast, flies fed with TMP continuously, from embryo to adult, showed low GFP expression throughout the course of the experiment (Figure 2B2, C2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B2, C2.

claim: Flies raised on regular fly food throughout show high GFP expression.
source: Furthermore, flies that were raised on regular fly food throughout showed high GFP expression (Figure 2B3, C3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B3, C3.

claim: A difference in GFP expression between flies raised on TMP and those switched to solvent-containing food is observed starting at one day post-eclosion.
source: We observed a difference between flies raised on TMP and those switched to solvent-containing food starting at one day post-eclosion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: No GFP expression is detected in flies younger than eight hours for either TMP or solvent condition.
source: However, we did not detect any GFP expression in flies younger than eight hours for either condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The lack of GFP expression even in the absence of TMP in young flies is most likely due to the time required to inactivate GAL80-DD upon TMP withdrawal.
source: This lack of GFP expression even in the absence of TMP is most likely due to the time that is required to inactivate GAL80-DD upon TMP withdrawal (Figure 1H), although it is formally possible that the expression level of Orco-Gal4 is low at eclosion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GFP degradation kinetics shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Fusion of the ecDHFR-derived destabilizing domain to GAL80 permits TMP to control GAL80 activity.
source: Either way, these results suggest that fusion of the ecDHFR-derived destabilizing domain to GAL80 permits TMP to control GAL80 activity, providing a chemically inducible system to control gene transcription in a temporal manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing TMP-dependent suppression of GAL4-driven expression.

claim: Olfactory aversion to CO2 can be abolished by silencing Gr21a-expressing sensory neurons.
source: Olfactory aversion to CO2 can be abolished by silencing Gr21a-expressing sensory neurons (Suh et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Suh et al., 2004.

claim: Gr21a-GAL4-derived tetanus toxin expression is blocked in the presence of GAL80-DD when flies are fed TMP, but not when they are fed solvent.
source: Gr21a-GAL4-derived tetanus toxin expression was blocked in the presence of GAL80-DD when flies were fed TMP, but not when they were fed the solvent (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Aversion to CO2 is observed only when flies expressing Gr21a-GAL4, UAS-TNT, nsyb-GAL80-DD are fed with TMP, and not when they are fed with solvent.
source: Accordingly, aversion to CO2 was observed only when flies expressing Gr21a-GAL4, UAS-TNT, nsyb-GAL80-DD were fed with TMP, and not when they were fed with the solvent (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Control flies with GAL4 alone have high avoidance for both solvent and TMP feeding conditions.
source: In comparison, control flies with GAL4 alone had high avoidance for both solvent and TMP feeding conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: GAL80-DD can be used to manipulate GAL4-dependent expression of neuronal effectors and thereby alter the function of neuronal circuits underlying behavior.
source: In summary, we show that GAL80-DD can be used to manipulate GAL4-dependent expression of neuronal effectors and thereby alter the function of neuronal circuits underlying behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by the CO2 avoidance behavioral data.

claim: Flippase-mediated removal of a stop cassette has been widely used for lineage analysis and sparse neuronal labeling.
source: Flippase-mediated removal of a stop cassette has been widely used for lineage analysis and sparse neuronal labeling (Lee and Luo, 1999; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee and Luo, 1999; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).

claim: Lineage analysis requires transient high-level expression of flippase (FLP) at specific developmental stages.
source: Lineage analysis requires transient high-level expression of flippase (FLP) at specific developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about lineage analysis techniques.

claim: Sparse neuronal labeling requires low-level FLP expression in post-mitotic neurons for the stochastic removal of a stop cassette.
source: On the other hand, sparse neuronal labeling requires low-level FLP expression in post-mitotic neurons for the stochastic removal of a stop cassette.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sparse labeling techniques.

claim: The number of GFP-positive olfactory projection neurons is correlated to the TMP dosage.
source: We observed that the number of GFP-positive olfactory projection neurons was correlated to the TMP dosage (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: By varying the concentration of TMP (0.01–1 mM) in fly food, the number of labeled projection neurons can be controlled.
source: By varying the concentration of TMP (0.01–1 mM) in fly food, we could control the number of labeled projection neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There are similar numbers of labeled neurons in both brain hemispheres for a given sample.
source: Furthermore, there were similar numbers of labeled neurons in both brain hemispheres for a given sample (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For flies fed with standard fly food without TMP, 42% of the brain hemispheres have only one GFP-positive cell.
source: For flies fed with standard fly food without TMP, 42% of the brain hemispheres had only one GFP-positive cell (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Dose-dependent expression of FLP-DD can be used to control the number of genetically manipulated cells within a population.
source: In summary, dose-dependent expression of FLP-DD can be used to control the number of genetically manipulated cells within a population.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent labeling.

claim: The expression patterns for NP21-GAL4 and GH146-GAL4 overlap only in the DA1 lateral projection neurons (lPNs) in the adult brain.
source: It has been reported that the expression patterns for NP21-GAL4 and GH146-GAL4 overlap only in the DA1 lateral projection neurons (lPNs) in the adult brain (Potter et al., 2010), which we validated (Figure 4A1,A2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Potter et al., 2010 and validated by experimental data shown in Figure 4A1,A2.

claim: When UAS-FLP expression is driven by NP21-GAL4, the adult intersection pattern includes additional olfactory projection neurons, ellipsoid body neurons and neurons with cell bodies close to the lateral horn.
source: However, when UAS-FLP expression is driven by NP21-GAL4, the adult intersection pattern includes additional olfactory projection neurons, ellipsoid body neurons and neurons with cell bodies close to the lateral horn (Figure 4B1,B2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B1,B2.

claim: When QUAS-FLP is driven by GH146-QF, the adult intersection pattern includes additional neurons (visual projection neurons).
source: Similarly, when QUAS-FLP is driven by GH146-QF, the adult intersection pattern includes additional neurons (visual projection neurons in this case) (Figure 4C1,C2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C1,C2.

claim: The discrepancy between the overlap and the intersection patterns arises because of the broader expression patterns for GH146-QF and NP21-GAL4 before the adult stage.
source: This discrepancy between the overlap and the intersection patterns arises because of the broader expression patterns for GH146-QF and NP21-GAL4 before the adult stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that intersection patterns include more cells than overlap patterns.

claim: The stop cassette is prematurely excised during development in neurons outside of the overlapping adult pattern.
source: Thus, the stop cassette is prematurely excised during development in neurons outside of the overlapping adult pattern.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the broader expression patterns during development.

claim: When UAS-FLP-DD is expressed by the NP21-GAL4 line and 1 mM TMP is fed to flies only during the adult stage, GFP expression is limited only to DA1 lPNs in the whole brain.
source: Indeed, when UAS-FLP-DD was expressed by the NP21-GAL4 line and 1 mM TMP was fed to flies only during the adult stage, GFP expression was limited only to DA1 lPNs in the whole brain (Figure 4D1,D2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D1,D2.

claim: Flies fed with solvent alone do not have GFP expression in any neurons in the brain.
source: In comparison, flies fed with solvent alone did not have GFP expression in any neurons in the brain (Figure 4E1,E2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E1,E2.

claim: Flies fed with 1 mM TMP throughout development have GFP expression in additional olfactory projection neurons.
source: Furthermore, flies fed with 1 mM TMP throughout development have GFP expression in additional olfactory projection neurons (Figure 4F1,F2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F1,F2.

claim: The expression pattern in UAS-FLP-DD flies fed with 1 mM TMP throughout development is a subset of that observed with UAS-FLP flies.
source: We noted that the expression pattern in UAS-FLP-DD flies fed with 1 mM TMP throughout development was a subset of that observed with UAS-FLP flies (Figure 4B,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,F.

claim: TMP levels may decline in the fly brain during metamorphosis after the larvae stop feeding.
source: It is possible that TMP levels decline in the fly brain during metamorphosis after the larvae stop feeding.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that expression patterns differ between FLP and FLP-DD.

claim: Similar results regarding TMP decline during metamorphosis have been observed in the context of RU486-induced FLP activity.
source: In fact, similar results have been observed in the context of RU486-induced FLP activity (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Feeding flies with 10 mM TMP throughout the larval stage results in a larger portion of the UAS-FLP expression pattern.
source: To mitigate this potential decline of TMP, we fed flies with 10 mM TMP throughout the larval stage and obtained a larger portion of the UAS-FLP expression pattern (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TMP can be used to limit FLP-DD activity temporally such that the intersection pattern is identical to the overlap in the adult expression patterns.
source: In sum, we show that TMP can be used to limit FLP-DD activity temporally in a way such that the intersection pattern is identical to the overlap in the adult expression patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing restricted expression to DA1 lPNs when TMP is fed only in adults.

claim: The DD system provides an independent axis of control which can be used in combination with existing reagents.
source: The DD system broadens the functionality of the Drosophila genetic toolkit as it provides an independent axis of control which can be used in combination with existing reagents.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the demonstrated compatibility with multiple binary systems.

claim: TMP-induced DD stabilization is dose-dependent over several orders of magnitude of TMP concentration.
source: First, TMP-induced DD stabilization is dose-dependent over several orders of magnitude of TMP concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: Tools such as GAL80-DD can be combined with existing GAL4 lines to knockdown targeted genes by RNAi or to perform neuronal silencing screens in a temporally refined manner.
source: Second, in contrast to existing chemical reagents, tools such as GAL80-DD can be combined with existing GAL4 lines to knockdown targeted genes by RNAi or to perform neuronal silencing screens in a temporally refined manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the demonstrated functionality of GAL80-DD with existing GAL4 lines.

claim: The degradation kinetics of the DD fusion protein are most likely faster than those of the native protein when TMP is withdrawn.
source: Third, when TMP is withdrawn, the degradation kinetics of the DD fusion protein are most likely faster than those of the native protein.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the mechanism of DD-mediated degradation.

claim: The DD system may offer fast temporal control in experiments which require reversible gene expression.
source: Thus, it is possible that the DD system offers fast temporal control in experiments which require reversible gene expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the degradation kinetics.

claim: The cost of TMP is almost 150 times less than RU486 or quinic acid at their respective working concentrations.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that the cost of TMP is almost 150 times less than RU486 or quinic acid at their respective working concentrations, making the DD system conducive to large scale behavioral screens.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of chemical costs.

claim: The applicability of the DD system for a given cell type is limited by two factors: the cell type should have an active proteasome, and orally-fed TMP should be able to reach the cell.
source: The applicability of the DD system for a given cell type is limited by two factors: (1) the cell type should have an active proteasome; (2) orally-fed TMP should be able to reach the cell.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mechanism of the DD system.

claim: Low proteasome activity may result in high residual levels of the chimeric protein in the absence of TMP.
source: In the absence of TMP, the level of proteasome activity in a given cell type may influence the residual level of a DD chimeric protein. For instance, low proteasome activity may result in high residual levels of the chimeric protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mechanism of proteasome-mediated degradation.

claim: It may be possible to reduce residual expression by co-expressing components of the protein degradation machinery.
source: It may be possible to reduce the residual expression by co-expressing components of the protein degradation machinery, similar to how co-expression of Dicer enhances RNAi efficiency (Dietzl et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on analogy to RNAi enhancement strategies.

claim: TMP is a cell-permeable ligand which can cross the blood-brain barrier.
source: As TMP is a cell-permeable ligand which can cross the blood-brain barrier, it should be accessible to all tissues during the adult and larval stages.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about TMP properties.

claim: The effectiveness of TMP in stabilizing the protein of interest during late pupal stages is reduced due to lack of feeding for several days leading up to this stage.
source: However, the effectiveness of TMP in stabilizing the protein of interest during late pupal stages is reduced due to lack of feeding for several days leading up to this stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and knowledge about pupal development.

claim: The level of gene expression controlled by GAL80-DD should always be determined using reporters before manipulating neuronal activity with effector transgenes.
source: Therefore, the level of gene expression controlled by GAL80-DD should always be determined using reporters before manipulating neuronal activity with effector transgenes.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the potential for leaky expression during late pupal stages.

claim: It will take roughly 24 hr to activate or inactivate the DD-system to an appreciable degree.
source: We anticipate that it will take roughly 24 hr to activate or inactivate the DD-system to an appreciable degree.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinetics data shown in the results.

claim: DMSO at concentrations greater than 0.1% has a detrimental effect on the survival of larvae.
source: During the course of our experiments, we observed a detrimental effect of the solvent DMSO (greater than 0.1%) on the survival of larvae (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic.
source: Finally, as trimethoprim is an antibiotic, experiments using the DD system should incorporate appropriate controls to rule out the effect of gut microbes on the phenotype of interest.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about trimethoprim.

claim: GAL80-DD is the first construct that allows control of GAL80 activity in vivo by a small molecule.
source: To our knowledge, GAL80-DD is the first construct that allows control of GAL80 activity in vivo by a small molecule.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: GAL80ts may be preferable in experiments that require low background expression.
source: While GAL80ts may still be preferable in experiments that require low background expression, GAL80-DD is a useful alternative for experiments that are disrupted by temperature manipulations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of the two systems.

claim: An RU486-inducible FLP recombinase was constructed by fusing it with the human progesterone receptor (Flp-Switch).
source: In a previous study, an RU486-inducible FLP recombinase was constructed by fusing it with the human progesterone receptor (Flp-Switch) (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: All DD-fusion proteins presented in this study are soluble molecules which function in the cytoplasm or the nucleus.
source: All DD-fusion proteins presented in this study are soluble molecules which function in the cytoplasm or the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the constructs presented.

claim: Previous studies have used ecDHFR-derived destabilized domains to conditionally alter membrane protein expression.
source: However, previous studies have used ecDHFR-derived destabilized domains to conditionally alter membrane protein expression (Iwamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iwamoto et al., 2010.

claim: The DD technology can be used to temporally control expression of membrane proteins such as ion channels and G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: Therefore, we predict that this tool can be used to temporally control expression of membrane proteins such as ion channels and G-protein-coupled receptors.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on previous studies with membrane proteins.

claim: DD can be knocked-in and fused to endogenous proteins to control their expression by limiting TMP feeding.
source: DD can be knocked-in and fused to endogenous proteins to control their expression by limiting TMP feeding.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications.

claim: DD knock-in can be done using custom-designed genome editing strategies or by integration into available MiMIC sites within coding introns.
source: This can be done using custom-designed genome editing strategies or by integration into the large number of available MiMIC sites within coding introns (Venken et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established genome editing techniques and citation to Venken et al., 2011.

claim: DD can be fused to a variety of effector genes for the purpose of inducible neuronal silencing or genome editing.
source: DD can also be fused to a variety of effector genes for the purpose of inducible neuronal silencing or genome editing (Maji et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications, with citation to Maji et al., 2017.

claim: GFP-DD can be coupled with knock-in GAL4 lines to compare gene expression in individual cells across time points spanning only a few hours.
source: Due to its inducible nature, GFP-DD can be coupled with knock-in GAL4 lines to compare gene expression in individual cells across time points spanning only a few hours, such as circadian fluctuation of gene expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications.

claim: GFP-DD may be useful as a sensor for proteasome activity.
source: GFP-DD may also be useful as a sensor for proteasome activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications.

claim: Temperature can have a significant impact on the physiology and behavior of a fly.
source: First, temperature can have a significant impact on the physiology and behavior of a fly (Parisky et al., 2016; Sigrist et al., 2003), which may prevent detection of the phenotype of interest.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Parisky et al., 2016 and Sigrist et al., 2003.

claim: Temperature-dependent tools are unlikely to be suitable for the study of thermosensory circuits and related behaviors.
source: For example, temperature-dependent tools are unlikely to be suitable for the study of thermosensory circuits and related behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the impact of temperature on fly physiology and behavior.

claim: Temporal control of gene expression using GAL80ts can only be achieved with transcription factors containing the GAD-activation domain.
source: Second, temporal control of gene expression using GAL80ts can only be achieved with transcription factors containing the GAD-activation domain, making it incompatible with a majority of the driver lines (LexA, QF and split-GAL4) that do not have the GAD domain.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the mechanism of GAL80ts.

claim: GAL80ts is incompatible with a majority of driver lines (LexA, QF and split-GAL4) that do not have the GAD domain.
source: Second, temporal control of gene expression using GAL80ts can only be achieved with transcription factors containing the GAD-activation domain, making it incompatible with a majority of the driver lines (LexA, QF and split-GAL4) that do not have the GAD domain.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the structure of different driver lines.

claim: Application of current chemical-dependent tools requires the generation of new transgenic stocks, such as new promoter-GAL4 lines.
source: Third, application of the current chemical-dependent tools requires the generation of new transgenic stocks, such as new promoter-GAL4 lines.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about existing chemical-dependent systems.

claim: RU486 has been reported to cause developmental lethality in flies with pan-neuronal expression of the RU486-sensitive GAL4.
source: Additionally, RU486, a chemical used to induce gene expression in the Geneswitch system, has been reported to cause developmental lethality in flies with pan-neuronal expression of the RU486-sensitive GAL4 (Li and Stavropoulos, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li and Stavropoulos, 2016.

claim: A recent study demonstrated that TMP can regulate activity of the yeast I-SceI endonuclease in Drosophila larvae expressing the fusion protein I-SceI-DD.
source: A recent study demonstrated that TMP can regulate activity of the yeast I-SceI endonuclease in Drosophila larvae expressing the fusion protein I-SceI-DD (Janssen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Janssen et al., 2016.

claim: Differences in GFP expression between solvent and TMP fed flies are significant across all developmental stages tested.
source: Differences in GFP expression between solvent and TMP fed flies are significant (unpaired t-test, two-tailed) across all developmental stages - Larva (p<0.001, t = 18.6, n = 6), Early pupa (p<0.001, t = 10.89, n = 5–6), Late pupa (p=0.025, t = 3.46, n = 5–6), Adult at eclosion (p=0.022, t = 3.25, n = 6), 3 day old adult (p<0.001, t = 7.55, n = 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Differences in GFP expression between solvent and TMP-fed flies are significant for all cell-types tested (n = 4–6, p<0.003, t > 5.3).
source: Differences in GFP expression between solvent and TMP-fed flies are significant for all cell-types shown (n = 4–6, p<0.003, t > 5.3, unpaired t-test, two-tailed, for all cell types).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 1% DMSO severely affects survival of larvae.
source: 1% DMSO was found to severely affect survival of larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.
